notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 30, drawn from the sources I was able to read.

---

## Exodus 30 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Section 1: The Altar of Incense (vv. 1–10)

**v. 1 — "You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense."**
The altar had one exclusive purpose — burning incense. No sacrifices were to be offered on it. The Hebrew expression is *mizbeakh miqtar qetoret*, which specifies the kind of altar this is: an altar for burning incense (or "an incense-altar of incense"). The Hebrew word for altar (*mizbeakh*, from *zabakh*, "to slay") normally carries the idea of slain sacrifices, so a qualifying term is added because no animal sacrifice was performed here. Ellicott notes that the placement of this instruction here (rather than with the other furniture in Exodus 25) is unexplained, but there is no reason to suspect textual dislocation. David Thompson (quoted at Precept Austin) suggests that until the priests were ordained and everything was in place, the whole operation was not yet a sweet-smelling fragrance to God; so instructions for the incense altar are given after the priestly ordination instructions.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 2 — "It is to be square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns must be of one piece."**
The altar measured about 18 inches (0.5 m) square and 36 inches (1 m) high. It was much smaller than the brazen altar in the courtyard (which was five cubits square and three cubits high). The horns, like those on the bronze altar (Ex 27:2), were projections at the four corners, carved from the same piece of wood, not attached separately. Ellicott observes that this small surface was ample for burning a precious material that could only be offered in small quantities.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 3 — "Overlay with pure gold the top and all the sides and horns, and make a molding of gold around it."**
It was overlaid entirely with pure gold — top, sides, and horns. Items closest to the Ark were covered with the most precious metal. Next to the Ark of the Covenant, the altar of incense was the most holy article of furniture. Ellicott notes it symbolised both prayer (in its general use) and expiation (when blood was applied to its horns). The "molding" (KJV: "crown of gold") was a raised rim or edging to prevent what was on top from falling off — like the molding on the table of showbread (Ex 25:24).
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 4 — "And make two gold rings below the molding on opposite sides to hold the poles used to carry it."**
Since the altar was small and light, only two rings were needed (contrast the four rings on the larger brazen altar, Ex 27:4). The rings were placed under the gold molding on opposite sides. As Currid notes (cited at Precept Austin), like the Ark, the altar was not to be touched by human hands; it was carried by poles inserted through these rings.
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 5 — "Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold."**
Same construction as the Ark's poles (Ex 25:13). Notably, unlike the Ark, the poles of the incense altar are not stated as remaining permanently in place (Ex 25:15 required the Ark's poles to stay in the rings).
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary

**v. 6 — "Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony—before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony—where I will meet with you."**
The altar stood in the Holy Place, outside the veil, but directly in front of the mercy seat within the Holy of Holies. The priest burning incense could not see the mercy seat, but faced toward it. JFB comments that this taught that though we cannot with the eye of sense see the throne of grace, we must "direct our prayer to it and look up" (cf. Ps 5:3). The writer of Hebrews (9:4) speaks of the golden altar as belonging in a certain sense to the Holy of Holies because of this close association. Guzik notes that it was positioned with the table of showbread (communion with God) and the lampstand (testimony to the world), completing the triad: the golden altar speaks of the offering of adoration.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/exodus/30.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**vv. 7–8 — "And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come."**
Incense was to be burned twice daily: in the morning when the lamps were trimmed, and at twilight when the lamps were lit. Both occasions coincided with the morning and evening sacrifices. JFB comments that from the uniform combination of these two services, incense was an emblem of the prayers of sincere worshippers ascending to heaven. The priest at this altar typified the intercessory office of Christ (Luke 1:10; Heb 7:25). The Expositor's Bible Commentary adds that incense — matter passing into the immaterial — is "the sigh of the sensuous for the spiritual state of being; it is an aspiration."
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/exodus/30.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-30.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/

**v. 9 — "On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering; nor are you to pour a drink offering on it."**
"Strange incense" (KJV) meant any incense composed differently from the recipe given in vv. 34–35. No animal sacrifice, grain offering, or drink offering was permitted on this altar — those belonged to the brazen altar. Guzik draws the spiritual point: prayer is not the place where sacrificial atonement is made; it is the place where atonement is enjoyed. We do not save ourselves through prayer; we pray because of Jesus' saving work.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 10 — "Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar... with the blood of the sin offering of atonement. The altar is most holy to the LORD."**
On the Day of Atonement, the high priest sprinkled the blood of the sin offering on the horns of the incense altar (see Lev 16:18–19). Guzik stresses that this was where atonement was *remembered and enjoyed*, not *made*. Every day when priests approached to burn incense, they saw the blood-stained horns — a constant reminder that prayer depends on atoning blood, not human effort. Ellicott notes that this passage determines the sense of Leviticus 16:18, confirming the "altar before the Lord" is the incense altar, not the brazen altar.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

---

### Section 2: The Ransom Money (vv. 11–16)

**vv. 11–12 — "When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered."**
A census was dangerous because numbering people signified ownership — and Israel belonged to God alone. Without ransom money, a census communicated that a human king owned the people. This explains why David's unauthorized census in 2 Samuel 24 brought a plague: he counted without requiring the ransom payment. Guzik states, "A census without ransom money signified human ownership of Israel rather than God's." The NET Bible note (cited at Precept Austin) explains: those numbered among the redeemed of the Lord were to support the work of the Lord to maintain their fellowship with the covenant.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary

**v. 13 — "Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, which weighs twenty gerahs."**
The half-shekel was a small lump of silver, unstamped (coins were unknown in Moses' time), weighing about 110 grains troy. The "shekel of the sanctuary" was a standard weight kept by the priests, ensuring all offerings were measured consistently. A gerah was literally a "bean" (probably the carob bean), which became a weight unit — much like our "grain."
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 14 — "Everyone twenty years of age or older who crosses over must give this offering to the LORD."**
Twenty was the age of full adulthood in Israel: military service began at twenty (Num 1:3), and Levites commenced sanctuary service at twenty (1 Chron 23:24–27; Ezra 3:8).
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 15 — "The rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less."**
This was a flat-rate payment, not a tithe or free-will offering. All paid the same because all souls are equally precious to God, and all need the same redemption price. Citing Adam Clarke, Guzik notes: "all had sinned, and all must be redeemed by the same price." Morgan adds: "Here the rich and the poor stood upon a perfect equality." Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) says the payment confessed "that he deserved to die, owning that he was in debt to God."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/

**v. 16 — "Take the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting. It will serve as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives."**
The silver (over 100 talents, about four tons) was used for the sockets supporting the tabernacle boards, the hooks, capitals, and connecting rods (Ex 38:27–28). Thus the ransom money literally held the tabernacle together. Ellicott notes that as long as the tabernacle stood, the silver remained in sight as a continual "memorial" — a reminder of their covenant position with God. Gill adds that it reminded them they were sinners whose lives were forfeited, that a ransom price was given and accepted, and that atonement (in a typical sense) was made.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/30-16.html

---

### Section 3: The Bronze Basin (vv. 17–21)

**v. 18 — "You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it."**
The laver (basin) had no specified dimensions. It was a large urn or vase supported on a stem rising from a pedestal (similar to those in Assyrian bas-reliefs). It was placed between the brazen altar and the entrance to the tabernacle — Jewish tradition says slightly to the south. The bronze came from the mirrors of the women of Israel (Ex 38:8). Guzik observes it was wonderful that people gave up "the measure of their own appearance for God's cleansing."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**vv. 19–20 — "Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet... so that they will not die."**
Washing the hands symbolised purity in act; washing the feet, holiness in walk and conversation (Ellicott). The priests had to wash both before entering the Holy Place and before ministering at the altar. Guzik connects this to Psalm 24:3–4 ("clean hands and a pure heart") and to Jesus washing the disciples' feet (John 13:10): "He who is bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean." The ongoing washing corresponds to cleansing through God's Word — "the washing of water by the word" (Eph 5:26). The death penalty for neglect was severe but, as Ellicott notes, "ablution was so easy... that to omit it would imply intentional disrespect towards God."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**v. 21 — "This shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come."**
The external act was to continue as long as the Levitical dispensation lasted; the internal purity it symbolised would be required of those who enter God's presence forever (cf. Heb 12:14). Gill notes this lasted until the Messiah came "and washed all his people, his priests, with his own blood, from all their sins" (Rev 1:5).
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/30-21.html

---

### Section 4: The Holy Anointing Oil (vv. 22–33)

**vv. 23–25 — "Take the finest spices: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount (250 shekels) of fragrant cinnamon, 250 shekels of fragrant cane, 500 shekels of cassia... and a hin of olive oil. Prepare from these a sacred anointing oil."**
Ellicott provides detailed notes on each ingredient: "pure myrrh" (lit. "myrrh of freedom") was the finest, freely exuding kind, not the inferior type from bark incisions. Cinnamon was one of the rarest spices in the ancient world, obtained from the *laurus cinnamomum* tree, likely imported from India or Ceylon via Arabia. Sweet calamus (fragrant cane) is an aromatic reed of uncertain species. Cassia (*kiddah*) is the inner bark of the *cinnamomum cassia* tree, more pungent than cinnamon. A hin of olive oil is about one gallon (3.7 litres). The mixture was to be compounded "after the art of the perfumer" — the best skill of the time was employed, with Jewish tradition saying the essence was first extracted from each spice, then mixed with oil.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**vv. 26–29 — "Use this oil to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark... the table... the lampstand... the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering... and the basin with its stand."**
Everything was consecrated with the oil: first the tabernacle itself, then its furniture — starting with the Ark in the Most Holy Place, then the Holy Place items (table, lampstand, incense altar), then the courtyard items (brazen altar, laver). The anointing set them apart as most holy. "Whatever touches them shall be holy" means that anything coming into contact with these consecrated objects became devoted to God and could not be put to common use.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/

**v. 30 — "Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests."**
The anointing of persons came after the anointing of objects. As Ellicott notes, just as Aaron and his sons were unfit to minister until the holy oil was poured on them, Christian ministers can only be fitted for their office by receiving the effluence of the Holy Spirit that the oil typified.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**vv. 31–33 — "This will be My sacred anointing oil for the generations to come. It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man... Anyone who mixes perfume like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people."**
The oil was exclusively for sacred use. Guzik sees oil as emblematic of the Holy Spirit: it "is not poured out to enhance our flesh, but to glorify Himself." The ban on imitation teaches that the work of the Holy Spirit is never to be imitated; man-made substitutes for the gifts or operations of the Spirit deny His holiness. Gaebelein (cited at Precept Austin / StudyLight) concurs: the holy anointing oil is the type of the Holy Spirit needed for worship in the Spirit, and "the flesh is so corrupt that the Holy Spirit can have nothing to do with it."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-30.html

---

### Section 5: The Holy Incense (vv. 34–38)

**vv. 34–35 — "Take fragrant spices—gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense—in equal measures, and make a fragrant blend of incense... seasoned with salt, pure and holy."**
Ellicott identifies: stacte (gum resin) is probably gum storax from the *styrax officinalis* tree, common in Syria and Palestine. Onycha is thought to be the operculum (claw) of a mollusc (*unguis odoratus* or *blatta Byzantina*) from the Red Sea, which when burnt produces a strong odour. Galbanum is a gum with a strong pungent odour, disagreeable alone but which brings out and prolongs other scents. Frankincense was the main element, a gum from the *arbor thuris* tree. All were in equal measures. The mixture was "salted" — Cole (cited by Guzik) says this was probably to secure rapid burning (sodium chloride), perhaps also for preservation. Guzik also notes Clarke's practical observation that the fragrant incense counteracted the disagreeable smells from slaughtered animals, blood, and burning flesh.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/

**v. 36 — "Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you."**
The incense was to be ground very fine and placed before the Testimony — either on the golden altar or at its base, ready for offering. Ellicott says this symbolised the need of the perpetual offering of prayer. Gill notes that beating it fine helped it mix better, spread more easily on the coals, and cause the smoke to rise sooner. Its proximity to the divine presence made it "most holy."
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/30-36.html

**vv. 37–38 — "You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves... Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people."**
The same prohibition as for the anointing oil: the sacred compound could not be replicated for personal enjoyment. The penalty was being "cut off" — which the Pulpit Commentary interprets as "put to death by the civil authority" (cf. Ex 31:14). Guzik remarks that God was so concerned to protect the unique character of the tabernacle incense that He commanded excommunication for anyone who would make these holy things common. The sacred smell — symbolising the sweetness of prayer — was not to be used for human attraction or adornment.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/30-36.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

**Placement of the incense altar — Hebrews 9:4 debate.**
The writer of Hebrews says the Most Holy Place "had the golden altar of incense" (Heb 9:4). This has generated discussion because Exodus places the altar outside the veil. Ellicott (Anglican) explains that the altar was so closely associated with the Holy of Holies — directly in front of the mercy seat — that the author of Hebrews could speak of it as belonging, "in a certain sense," to the Holy of Holies. JFB (Reformed/Presbyterian) similarly sees it as occupying a spot "directly in front of the mercy seat" so that the priest looked toward it. This is broadly agreed across traditions; I did not find a sharp denominational divide on this point.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/exodus/30.htm

**Anointing oil as type of the Holy Spirit — Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis.**
David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic tradition) draws an explicit application: the prohibition against imitating the oil teaches that "there is to be no place for encouraging a man-made imitation of the gifts or operations of the Holy Spirit." Gaebelein (dispensational/Bible conference) likewise calls the oil "the type of the Holy Spirit" and warns against counterfeit manifestations. This typological reading is common across traditions, but the Pentecostal/Charismatic tradition applies it with particular force against what it sees as fleshly imitations of spiritual gifts.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-30.html

**Ransom money and New Covenant giving.**
Guzik (charismatic/evangelical) explicitly states the half-shekel is "not a pattern for our giving under the New Covenant," which "should be proportional" (1 Cor 16:2). This contrasts with some traditions that might see a stronger continuity between the temple tax and church offerings. The Bridgeway Bible Commentary (evangelical) emphasises the equality aspect: "before God the rich had no advantage over the poor… all had an equal share in the maintenance of the tabernacle."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-30.html

**The bronze laver and ongoing sanctification.**
While all traditions see cleansing typology here, Guzik (charismatic) emphasises the ongoing, daily nature: "not just initial salvation, but ongoing washing through God's Word as we live in a dusty world." This reflects the Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis on continual spiritual experience. Gaebelein connects the laver specifically to "self-judged and self-denied" living and the Word as a "looking-glass" (mirror, from Ex 38:8), reflecting a Keswick/holiness emphasis on daily surrender. The Expositor's Bible Commentary takes a more liturgical approach, connecting incense to the dangers of "rhetoric in the leader of extempore prayer" and "studied inflexions in the conductor of liturgical service" — a more Anglican concern.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-30.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-30.html

## Other Views and Modern Scholarship

**Why the altar of incense appears here rather than Exodus 25.**
The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) acknowledge this is a puzzle: "Why this section has been held until now is a mystery." The widespread critical view that it was composed later "does not answer the question, it merely moves the issue to the work of an editor rather than the author." N. M. Sarna (Jewish Publication Society) notes that all materials for these final items were anticipated in the donation list of Exodus 25:3–6 and that they were not needed for installing Aaron and his sons. Thompson (cited at Precept Austin) offers a theological rationale: until everything — including priests — was in place, the operation was not yet a sweet-smelling fragrance to God.
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary

**Incense altars in the Ancient Near East.**
Currid (cited at Precept Austin) notes that incense altars have a long history in the ancient Near East. The earliest example in Palestine was discovered at et-Tell from the Early Bronze III period (c. 2650–2350 BC). They have been found in specifically Israelite contexts, such as Iron Age Arad. George Bush (19th-century commentator, also cited at Precept Austin) adds that incense altars appear in the most ancient Egyptian paintings, and the Egyptians offered incense to the sun three times daily — resin in the morning, myrrh at noon, and an aromatic compound called *kypi* at sunset. The custom pervaded all religions of antiquity. Ellicott likewise observes that God "sanctioned in His worship an innocent rite, which natural reason had pointed out to man as fitting and appropriate."
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-30-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html

**"Tempered together" vs. "salted" (v. 35).**
A translation debate exists over the Hebrew word in v. 35. The LXX, Vulgate, and Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan render it "tempered together" (mixed). However, Ellicott notes that most modern scholars (Buxtorf, Gesenius, Lee, Rosenmüller, De Wette, Kalisch, Keil) render it "salted" or "mixed with salt." The word is capable of either meaning. Guzik sides with "salted," citing Cole's view that sodium chloride was added for rapid burning and preservation.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-30.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-30/

**Catholic and Orthodox readings.**
The search limit prevented fetching from Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Anglican) does comment on the incense as type of prayer, connecting it to the liturgical use of incense in traditional churches. The general typology — incense as prayer, oil as the Holy Spirit — is shared broadly across traditions including Catholic and Orthodox, where incense continues in liturgical use and chrism (consecrated oil) is central to sacraments of confirmation and ordination. These traditional readings were not accessible for detailed citation within the search limits.
